performers: The Modena Chamber Orchestra (source attribution; embedded tag differs)
intro: A sunny E-major refrain keeps returning between birdsong, running water and a thunderstorm. Vivaldi gives three violinists the bird calls and lets the bass fall silent beneath them.

sections.label: A · Spring arrives
sections.mNote: Full strings announce E major, then echo themselves softly

sections.label: B · Three violins sing
sections.mNote: Trills and answering calls above E and B

sections.label: C · Running water
sections.mNote: Violin semiquavers flow over repeated bass quavers

sections.label: D · Thunder and lightning
sections.mNote: The storm reaches C♯ minor; birdsong follows

sections.label: A′ · The refrain finds E major
sections.mNote: The bass descends through C♯, F♯, B and E

sections.label: A″ · E major and its echo
sections.mNote: The closing phrase returns, followed by its soft echo

cues.title: Spring announces itself
cues.text: The 1725 sonnet begins: “Giunt’é la Primavera e festosetti / La Salutan gl’Augei con lieto canto” — “Spring has arrived, and the birds joyfully greet her with happy song.” The strings announce E major in firm phrases, each answered by a soft echo.
cues.evidence: Sonnet accompanying Vivaldi’s Op. 8 (1725), letters A–B; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, I, bars 1–13: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301. The poems were published anonymously.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Water under the breeze
cues.text: “E i fonti allo Spirar de’ Zeffiretti / Con dolce mormorio Scorrono intanto” — “Meanwhile the streams flow with a sweet murmur beneath the little breezes.” The sonnet’s water runs in violin semiquavers; repeated bass notes keep it within E major.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter C; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 31–40: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A black cloak overhead
cues.text: “Vengon’ coprendo l’aer di nero amanto / E Lampi, e tuoni ad annuntiarla eletti” — “Lightning and thunder come, chosen to announce her, covering the sky with a black cloak.” Vivaldi’s storm hammers repeated notes beneath the solo violin’s racing arpeggios. The music reaches C♯ minor.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter D; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 44–59; harmonic route in José Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The birds come back
cues.text: “Indi tacendo questi, gl’Augelletti / Tornan’ di nuovo al lor canoro incanto” — “Then, when these fall silent, the little birds return to their enchanting song.” Their trills return in C♯ minor. A long C♯ underneath them replaces the earlier silence of the bass.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter E; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 59–65, including the sustained continuo C♯: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The last soft echo
cues.text: The full strings bring back the refrain’s closing phrase in E major. Vivaldi repeats it softly, then closes with B resolving to E in the bass. The birds have finished; the familiar tune gets the last word.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, I, closing tutti and piano echo, bars 76–82: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Three birds after the cadence
transitions.how: The bass resolves B to E and falls silent with the violas. Three violin lines remain, exchanging trills and short calls. Held E and B notes among the violins keep the birdsong in E major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, I, bars 13–27: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: The stream starts in E major
transitions.how: A shortened refrain closes with B resolving to E in the bass. The violins begin flowing semiquavers, marked piano, over repeated E quavers. The new scene keeps the same key and Allegro tempo.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 27–40, especially the change to piano at letter C: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: Thunder on the bass B
transitions.how: The refrain reaches B major. Its bass B becomes a barrage of repeated demisemiquavers, marked thunder; the solo violin answers with rapid arpeggios. The storm moves through E major towards C♯ minor, where the refrain’s closing phrase returns.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 40–59; key sequence in Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.

transitions.title: Four bass notes lead home
transitions.to: A′ · The refrain finds E major
transitions.how: The strings gather after the bird calls. The bass moves C♯–F♯–B–E beneath the refrain: C♯ minor, F♯ minor seventh, B seventh, E major. The repeated C♯ of the birdsong has become the first step in a descending-fifths progression.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 66–70; harmony shown in Rodríguez Alvira’s score example: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.

transitions.title: The strings reclaim the closing phrase
transitions.from: A′ · The refrain finds E major
transitions.to: A″ · E major and its echo
transitions.how: The last solo ends over E and B in the bass. The tutti resumes on E with the refrain’s closing phrase, then repeats it piano. B resolves to E beneath the final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, final solo and tutti, bars 70–82: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

voices: Organ and cello bass line (not realised continuo)

composer.epithet: He wrote concertos for the women of Venice’s Pietà, operas for its theatres, and a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 a twenty-five-year-old Venetian became a priest in March and a violin teacher in September. Antonio Vivaldi had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and continued helping with his career long after the son had become famous. Venice knew Antonio as il prete rosso, the red priest. His working places would be the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year: in 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 took him back. The music survived the office politics.
